papers.title: Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31385v1

summary.one_liner: Discovery and spectroscopic confirmation of the quasar EUCL J150452.291+625224.39 (J1504+6252) at z = 8.129, the first quasar confirmed at z > 8, with black hole mass and Eddington-ratio estimates from H-beta and Mg II broad lines.
summary.plain: This paper reports a very distant quasar, a bright object powered by a supermassive black hole, seen as it was about 630 million years after the Big Bang. The object was spotted in Euclid survey images and then confirmed with several telescopes, including JWST. The authors estimate the black hole weighs a few hundred million times the Sun's mass, while it is currently feeding on gas at a rate below its maximum.
summary.why: It pushes the known redshift record for quasars back by about 39 million years and suggests that more massive black holes from this early era may exist unseen. Whether it changes how black holes form is not settled by the text; it says the object needs either a heavy starting seed or unusually efficient early growth.
summary.background:
- Redshift (z): how much light from a distant object is stretched to longer wavelengths by cosmic expansion; larger z means further away and earlier in time. z = 8.13 is roughly 630 million years after the Big Bang.
- Quasar: a very luminous core of a galaxy powered by a supermassive black hole swallowing surrounding gas.
- Broad emission lines: bright spectral lines from fast-moving gas near the black hole; their width (FWHM) is used to estimate black hole mass.
- Mass estimates: these rely on empirical calibrations between line width, brightness and mass, so they carry large uncertainties (here about 0.4 dex, a factor of roughly 2.5).
- Eddington ratio: the current accretion rate relative to the maximum rate a black hole can sustain; "sub-Eddington" means feeding below that limit.
- Reionisation era: the period when the first luminous objects ionised the hydrogen fog filling the early universe.
- Euclid, JWST, Keck, HST, LBT: telescopes and surveys used for the discovery and follow-up.

papers.abstract: Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history. We present the discovery of EUCL J150452.291+625224.39 (J1504+6252), selected from Euclid Wide Survey imaging and spectroscopically confirmed as the first quasar at z > 8 through observations with Keck, HST, LBT, and JWST. J1504+6252 exhibits the defining spectral signatures of archetypal quasars at lower redshift, including a luminous blue power-law continuum and broad permitted emission lines, indicating a classical broad-line region. JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy yields a systemic redshift of z = 8.129 +/- 0.005, corresponding to 630 Myr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by about 39 Myr (6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch). From H-beta and Mg II, we measured intrinsic broad-line-region FWHM of 3160 +/- 270 and 3740 (+160/-170) km/s, respectively. A widely used single-epoch H-beta calibration gives a reference black hole mass of log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.56 +/- 0.43. Applying a range of calibrations to both Mg II and H-beta yields log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.33-8.89 and Eddington ratios of 0.12-0.44. Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth. The discovery of a mature, sub-Eddington quasar at z > 8 suggests that substantially more luminous quasars hosting similarly massive black holes may remain to be discovered. Conversely, previously known reionisation-era quasars may represent the rapidly accreting end of a broader population of already massive black holes spanning a wider range of accretion states.

papers.title: Tidally Induced Coda: Double Transients from Black Hole-Star Binary Encounters with Massive Black Holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31361v1

summary.one_liner: Few-body scattering simulations (SpaceHub) of stellar-mass black hole–star binaries passing near a massive black hole, quantifying outcomes including a tidally triggered micro-tidal disruption event and fitting formulae for its cross section and the delay between two flares.
summary.plain: This paper looks at what happens when a pair of objects, a stellar-mass black hole orbiting a normal star, flies close to a much heavier black hole at the centre of a galaxy. The gravity of the heavy black hole can stretch the pair's orbit into a very elongated shape, which may cause the star to be torn apart by its black hole partner. The authors ran many computer simulations to estimate how often each outcome happens and how long apart two resulting flashes of light would appear.
summary.why: The paper proposes that such events would show up as two flares separated by months, which could serve as a distinctive signature to look for in surveys. The abstract's estimated event rates (a few to about 100 per year within 40 Gpc) are model predictions that depend on the simulation assumptions, so they should be read as estimates rather than confirmed numbers.
summary.background:
- Massive black hole (MBH): a black hole with millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, typically at a galaxy's centre.
- Stellar-mass black hole: a black hole formed from a collapsed massive star, a few times to tens of times the Sun's mass.
- Binary: two objects orbiting each other under mutual gravity.
- Eccentricity: how stretched an orbit is; 0 is a circle, near 1 is a very long thin ellipse.
- Tidal disruption event (TDE): a star torn apart by the gravity of a black hole, producing a flash of light. The "micro" version here involves a stellar-mass black hole doing the tearing.
- Few-body scattering experiment: a numerical simulation of a small number of gravitating bodies interacting at close range.
- Cross section: an effective target area describing how likely an interaction is.

papers.abstract: Dense stellar environments surrounding massive black holes (MBHs) provide a natural setting for dynamical interactions that can produce transient electromagnetic and gravitational-wave sources. In particular, the tidal field of an MBH can strongly perturb binaries undergoing close encounters with it, driving their internal orbits to extreme eccentricities. Here, we investigate the outcomes of such interactions for binaries composed of a stellar-mass black hole (BH) and a star. Using direct few-body scattering experiments with the code SpaceHub, we explore hyperbolic encounters between BH-star binaries and MBHs. We systematically quantify the probabilities of different dynamical outcomes as functions of the binary orbital parameters and MBH mass, with particular emphasis on a channel in which the tidally induced eccentricity triggers a micro-tidal disruption event ($\mu$TDE), as the star is disrupted by its BH companion, followed by accretion of the stellar debris onto the MBH. We derive fitting formulae for the $\mu$TDE cross section and for the time delay between the two resulting flares, finding that the latter can be a few months for an MBH of $10^6\,M_\odot$. These double transients offer a distinctive observational signature of $\mu$TDEs. We estimate event rates ranging from a few to $\sim 100\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ within a luminosity distance of $40\,{\rm Gpc}$.

papers.title: The Sensitivity of Gamma-Ray Searches for Dark Matter Annihilation in Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies: the LSST Era and Beyond
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31130v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter whose gravity holds galaxies together; some models say pairs of its particles can annihilate and emit gamma rays.
- Dwarf galaxies: small, faint galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, which contain a lot of dark matter and little else that emits gamma rays, making them good targets.
- J-factor: a measure of how much dark matter lies along the line of sight toward a galaxy; a high J-factor means a brighter expected signal.
- LSST: the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time, a large sky survey expected to find many new faint satellites.
- Fermi-LAT: NASA's space gamma-ray telescope now in operation; APT is a proposed future instrument.
- Monte Carlo pipeline: a computer method that runs many random simulated realizations to estimate the spread of possible outcomes.
summary.one_liner: A forecast of how well gamma-ray telescopes (Fermi-LAT and the proposed APT) can constrain dark matter annihilation using Milky Way dwarf satellite galaxies, including the effect of the many satellites expected from LSST, via the BabyBison Monte Carlo pipeline.
summary.plain: Dark matter is thought to make up most of the mass in galaxies but cannot be seen directly. This paper asks how well gamma-ray telescopes could detect signs of dark matter particles destroying each other inside the small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, and how much new galaxies found by the upcoming LSST survey would help. The authors' main finding is that the new discoveries would give only modest improvements, typically below 20%, while rare cases with undiscovered, very dense satellites could give much larger gains.
summary.why: Dwarf galaxies are among the cleanest places to search for dark matter annihilation signals, so knowing what future surveys can and cannot deliver helps plan observations. The finding that a few high-density satellites dominate the results, rather than the total count, is a useful point for planning, though the text alone does not show how robust it is to modeling assumptions.

papers.abstract: We forecast the sensitivity of gamma-ray searches to dark matter annihilation in Milky Way satellite dwarf galaxies using BabyBison, a Monte Carlo pipeline combining cosmological satellite simulations and observational selection functions with a joint likelihood analysis of gamma-ray data. Although LSST is expected to substantially expand the catalog of known satellite galaxies, we find that these discoveries are likely to produce only modest improvements in the resulting dark matter annihilation constraints, typically below 20\%. Much more substantial gains are possible, however, in relatively rare realizations that contain yet-to-be-discovered satellites with large $J$-factors. These results reinforce the fact that indirect detection analyses using the population of dwarf galaxies are typically driven in large part by a small number of high-$J$-factor systems rather than by the total satellite count. We present projections for the sensitivity of Fermi-LAT and the proposed Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (APT) to dark matter annihilation, finding that a complete census of the Milky Way dwarf sample could enable such instruments to probe dark matter with masses up to the TeV scale. We also investigate the dark matter discovery potential of these instruments and project their ability to measure the properties of an annihilating dark matter particle.

papers.title: Multiphase Gas in the Ram-Pressure-Stripped Elliptical Galaxy NGC 1404
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29706v1

summary.background:
- Elliptical galaxy: a smooth, mostly old star population with little new star formation.
- Fornax Cluster: a nearby group of galaxies that holds a large volume of hot X-ray gas.
- Ram pressure stripping: gas is pushed out of a galaxy as it moves through surrounding gas, like rain blown off a moving car.
- Intracluster medium: the hot, thin gas between galaxies in a cluster.
- Warm ionized gas: gas heated to about ten thousand degrees, seen through its glow of hydrogen-alpha light.
- Mach number: the ratio of turbulent speed to the speed of sound in the gas; about 0.5 means turbulence is moderate.
- Kolmogorov turbulence: a standard statistical pattern for how energy cascades across scales in a turbulent fluid.
- Velocity structure function: a measure of how much gas velocity differs between points separated by a given distance.
- Power spectrum: a way of splitting brightness or velocity variations into their different sized components.
- Resonant scattering and line broadening: X-ray spectral effects used to infer gas motion.
summary.one_liner: Multi-instrument study (MUSE optical, Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray) of gas motions in the hot and warm phases of the ram-pressure-stripped elliptical galaxy NGC 1404 falling through the Fornax Cluster, finding a Mach number of about 0.48 and warm-gas velocity structure consistent with Kolmogorov turbulence.
summary.plain: This paper looks at NGC 1404, an elliptical galaxy moving through the hot gas filling the Fornax Cluster. The wind of that gas pushes on the galaxy's own gas, a process called ram pressure stripping. The authors combined optical and X-ray observations to measure how fast and how turbulently the gas moves, in both its hot and warm forms.
summary.why: It gives a measured case of how an outside environment can stir up a galaxy's gas and may help explain how cooling produces off-center warm gas. The text reports these measurements for one galaxy, so it is unclear how far the result applies to other galaxies or clusters.

papers.abstract: Galaxy groups and low-mass galaxy clusters are major sites of environment-driven galaxy evolution. NGC 1404 is an X-ray-bright early-type galaxy traveling through the intracluster medium of the nearby low-mass Fornax Cluster, and it hosts off-center warm ionized gas. With minimal ongoing stellar feedback and negligible active galactic nucleus feedback, NGC 1404 provides an ideal laboratory for constraining the impact of environmental processes on the thermodynamics of the interstellar medium. We analyzed VLT/MUSE, 506 ks Chandra ACIS, and 119 ks XMM-Newton RGS observations to quantify gas motions in both the hot and warm phases of NGC 1404. We probed the kinematics of the warm gas by deriving the velocity structure function (VSF) from MUSE H$\alpha$ integral-field spectroscopy. To measure the kinematics of the hot gas, we derived the power spectrum of X-ray surface brightness fluctuations from the Chandra data, and independently constrained galaxy-scale hot gas motions by measuring Fe XVII resonant scattering and turbulent line broadening with RGS. Our RGS spectral analysis gives a three-dimensional Mach number of $0.48^{+0.22}_{-0.14}$, consistent with the power-spectrum results from Chandra for the same extraction region, and corresponding to a turbulent-to-thermal energy density ratio of $\sim0.13$. The warm-gas VSF follows the expectation for Kolmogorov turbulence and is broadly consistent with the hot-gas kinematics. The off-center warm gas in NGC 1404 may have formed through radiative cooling of the hot interstellar medium, triggered by the uplift of low-entropy hot gas during ram pressure stripping. Our study suggests that ram pressure stripping can drive substantial gas motions and reshape the thermodynamic state of the interstellar medium of cluster member galaxies.

papers.title: The role of gas on the collisional runaway path to supermassive black hole seeds
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26885v1

summary.background:
- Supermassive black holes: black holes with millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, found at the centres of galaxies.
- Black hole "seeds": the smaller black holes that the largest ones are thought to grow from.
- Star cluster core collapse: the process in which stars in a dense cluster's centre sink and crowd together, speeding up collisions.
- Runaway collisions: stars merging repeatedly to form one very massive object that can collapse into a black hole.
- N-body simulation: a computer method that tracks the gravitational pull between many individual bodies (here, stars).
- SPH (smoothed particle hydrodynamics): a method that models gas as many small particles.
- Gas fraction: the share of the cluster's mass that is gas rather than stars.
- Dynamical friction: the drag that heavy objects feel as they move through a surrounding sea of lighter matter, which pulls them toward the centre.
summary.one_liner: Coupled N-body and SPH simulations (AMUSE, BRIDGE) of dense, gas-embedded star clusters test how gas fraction (0–20%) changes runaway stellar collisions and the mass of the resulting black hole seed.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how the very large black holes seen in the early universe might have started, specifically from tightly packed clusters of stars that merge together. The authors ran 48 computer simulations of such clusters, some containing gas, and tracked how stars collide. They report that more gas tended to produce a more massive central black hole, with the gain growing from about 8% at low gas fractions to about 44% at 20% gas.
summary.why: Supermassive black holes are observed at a time when the universe was young, and it is unclear how they grew so fast, so a possible seed-formation route is of interest. The result is limited to the simulated setups, and the authors say their simulations do not fully resolve the dynamical friction effect they mention, so the findings should be read as a model-based indication rather than a settled answer.

papers.abstract: The origin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remains unclear, despite observational evidence for their rapid formation in the early Universe, as evidenced by active galactic nuclei (AGN) at high redshift. In this paper, we investigate stellar dynamics in dense, gas-embedded clusters. We explore how gas influences the runaway collision process and the subsequent formation of SMBH seeds in a global instability scenario. We perform a series of coupled N-body and SPH simulations using the AMUSE framework, with the stellar and gaseous components interacting gravitationally via the BRIDGE method. We use 12 initial condition models with equal-mass stars following Plummer distributions, with total masses ranging from $10^3$ to $5 \times 10^5~M_{\odot}$, virial radii from $0.005$ to $0.1$ pc, and stellar masses of $1$, $10$ and $50$ $M_{\odot}$. For each model, we perform four simulations with gas fractions ranging from 0\% to 20\%, resulting in a total of 48 simulations. The gas is sampled with the same spatial distribution as the stars, with a mass ratio per particle of $m_{\rm SPH}/m = 0.01$, where $m$ is the stellar mass. We find that in most of our simulations, higher gas fractions lead to the formation of more massive black hole, as the core collapses earlier, triggering collisions through gas--star interactions. Our results show increases in BH mass of $\sim 8\%$ for low gas fractions, to $\sim 44\%$ at 20\% gas fraction. The core collapse time is also shortened, with the strongest reduction at $20\%$ gas fraction ($\sim 27\%$). The transonic regime of our initial conditions is where dynamical friction is most efficient in principle. Although our simulations do not fully resolve this effect, gas--star interactions are the principal mechanism driving the enhancement in BH formation efficiency, in the absence of other dissipation mechanisms.

papers.title: An early interaction between the Sagittarius dwarf and the Milky Way I: Fossil signatures in the phase-space structure of the disc
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27898v1

summary.background:
- Milky Way disc: the flat, rotating plane of stars containing the Sun.
- Sagittarius dwarf: a small galaxy being absorbed by the Milky Way; its orbit is thought to have passed through the disc in the past.
- N-body plus hydro simulation: a computer model tracking many gravitating particles (stars, dark matter) and gas over time.
- Phase-space structure: the joint map of where stars are and how fast they move.
- Vertical velocity dispersion: the spread of stars' up-and-down speeds; a higher value means the stars are being heated.
- Age-velocity dispersion relation: how the up-and-down spread grows with stellar age, a clock for disc heating.
- Thickening: stars spreading further above and below the disc plane.
- Low-alpha disc: a chemically defined, younger-looking population of Milky Way stars, identified by abundance ratios.
- Pericentre: the closest approach of an orbiting object to the centre of the host.
summary.one_liner: Using four controlled N-body plus hydrodynamic simulations of a Milky-Way-like galaxy hit by a Sagittarius-like dwarf on a polar orbit, this paper shows that a single early disc crossing thickens and heats the age-resolved thin disc in a datable way, and that the fiducial run's dispersion jump roughly matches the outer low-alpha disc observed by Das et al. (2024).
summary.plain: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, may have been brushed by the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy, a smaller neighbour, about 5 to 7 billion years ago. The authors ran computer simulations of that encounter and checked how the stars in the galaxy's flat disc were shaken up. They found that stars already present during the pass were puffed up and sped up in their up-and-down motion, while stars born later were not affected.
summary.why: If the disc keeps a lasting, age-dated record of one passing satellite, stellar ages and motions could be used to date past encounters and estimate the mass of the visitor. The authors say the mass-from-jump inversion is only good to about a factor of 1.5, so the link to the real satellite is approximate.

papers.abstract: Several independent lines of evidence point to an early encounter between the Milky Way and the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy $5$-$7$ Gyr ago. We present four controlled $N$-body+hydro simulations, one of an isolated host galaxy and three of a single interaction between a Milky-Way-like host and a Sagittarius-like satellite on an unbound polar orbit. Relative to the fiducial satellite (with total mass $0.7\times10^{11}$ M$_\odot$), one run increases the satellite's mass by a factor of $1.5$ and another its crossing speed by a factor of $1.4$, giving pericentric speeds of $466$-$634$ km s$^{-1}$ at pericentric radii of $R\simeq15$-$18$ kpc. Comparing the present-day, phase-space structure in radial bins by age of newly-formed thin-disc stars across the runs, we find that stars that existed at the time of the passage are thickened by up to $\sim37$ per cent in mass-enclosed height and heated by up to $\sim5$ km s$^{-1}$ in vertical velocity dispersion relative to the control, while stars formed after the passage are unaffected. The heating signature is also evident when comparing the age-vertical velocity dispersion relation against a heating relation with a power law of $0.38$, obtained by fitting the isolated host. A single, disc crossing from an early interaction thus suffices to leave lasting, datable fossils in the age-resolved vertical structure of a galactic disc. The fiducial run's dispersion jump of $\sim4$ km s$^{-1}$ matches best with that observed in the outer low-$\alpha$ disc of the Milky Way (Das et al. 2024), corresponding to a perturber mass of $0.7\times10^{11}$ M$_\odot$, with a velocity of $466$ km s$^{-1}$ at a pericentric radius of $16.7$ kpc, though the inversion from jump amplitude to perturber mass is good only to a factor of $\sim1.5$.

papers.title: Disentangling Disk and Broad-Line Region Continuum Emission in a Sample of Active Galactic Nuclei
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27051v1

summary.background:
- Active galactic nucleus (AGN): a galaxy core with a supermassive black hole accreting gas, very bright in its centre.
- Accretion disk: a hot, flat disk of gas spiralling into the black hole; it emits mostly blue/ultraviolet light.
- Broad-line region (BLR): a cloud of fast-moving gas near the black hole that produces broad emission lines in spectra.
- Diffuse continuum (DC): smooth light emitted by that gas, which adds to the disk light and shows features (jumps) at specific wavelengths.
- Balmer and Paschen jumps: sudden steps in brightness at fixed wavelengths set by atomic hydrogen energy levels; they act as fingerprints of the gas glow.
- Reverberation mapping: measuring time delays between brightness changes in different colours to infer the size of emitting regions.
- Spectral decomposition: splitting a measured spectrum into separate known components (disk, gas glow, emission lines).
- Cloudy: a widely used computer code that simulates radiation from gas; LOC (locally optimally-emitting clouds) is a model of the cloud population.
summary.one_liner: Using source-specific Cloudy/LOC diffuse-continuum templates fitted to HST/STIS and VLT/X-shooter spectra of 31 AGNs, this paper quantifies the Balmer- and Paschen-jump diffuse continuum fraction from the broad-line region and tests how template choice biases the inferred disk-plus-DC decomposition.
summary.plain: Bright galaxy cores (active galactic nuclei, powered by material falling onto a central black hole) emit light that varies over time, and astronomers track how these changes arrive across colours. This study looks at the light in 31 such cores and asks how much of the smooth glow comes from hot gas near the black hole rather than from the accretion disk itself. The authors build a model of that gas glow for each object and fit it to the spectra, finding that on average about a third of the light just below the Balmer jump (a sharp step in the spectrum near 3625 Å) comes from this gas.
summary.why: Earlier timing measurements suggested the disk is larger than simple models predict, and the gas glow may explain part of that mismatch and an extra blue excess. The paper also shows that a poorly chosen template can bias the inferred fraction, so the result matters for how future studies separate the disk from the gas. The link to the timing puzzle is suggested by the text rather than fully demonstrated here.

papers.abstract: Recent continuum reverberation-mapping measurements of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) indicate that the inter-band time lags are significantly larger than those predicted by the light travel times across the standard thin model. In addition, the observed $u$-band excess suggests the presence of diffuse continuum (DC) radiation originating in the broad-line region (BLR). Spectroscopically, the Balmer and Paschen jumps in DC emission are unique indicators to quantify the contributions of the BLR to the observed continuum. Here, we study the DC contributions of 31 AGNs, whose spectra are obtained with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and with X-shooter on the Very Large Telescope (VLT). In each spectrum, at least one of the Balmer and Paschen jumps is covered. For each object, we performed radiative transfer calculations using Cloudy within the Locally Optimally-emitting Clouds (LOC) model to construct source-specific DC spectral templates. We quantified the DC contribution by incorporating these templates as continuum components in spectral decomposition. The average ratio of the DC to total (i.e., disk+DC) continua is ~33% just below the Balmer jump (~3625 Å). The Balmer jump provides a stronger constraint on the DC component than the Paschen jump. Simulations based on mock spectra further demonstrate that an unsuitable template can introduce systematic, wavelength-dependent biases to the inferred DC fraction. Our results underscore the importance of employing appropriate DC templates in the spectral decomposition to infer the substantial DC contribution. Upcoming time-resolved spectra will enable more detailed modelling and tighter constraints on the disk and BLR.

papers.title: High-precision proper motions toward the Galactic bulge Baade's window from a decade of DECam observations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26961v1

summary.background:
- Proper motion: the yearly apparent drift of a star across the sky, measured in milliarcseconds per year.
- Galactic bulge: the dense central region of the Milky Way, where dust and crowding make observations hard.
- Baade's window: a relatively clear, low-dust line of sight toward the bulge often used for study.
- DECam: a large digital camera on a telescope in Chile, built from many CCD chips (detectors).
- Gaia DR3: a European space-telescope catalogue of positions and motions used here as the reference frame.
- Velocity dispersion: the spread of stellar motions, a measure of how randomly stars move.
- Color-magnitude diagram: a plot of star brightness against colour, used to infer stellar ages.
- Main-sequence turnoff: the point on that plot where stars begin leaving the main stable phase; its position indicates age.
- Foreground contamination: nearby disk stars along the same line of sight that are not part of the bulge.
summary.one_liner: A pilot study measuring proper motions (apparent sky drift over time) of stars in one DECam detector field toward Baade's window in the Galactic bulge, using about 10 years of r-band data tied to the Gaia DR3 frame, with velocity dispersions and a color-magnitude diagram of the bulge population.
summary.plain: Astronomers wanted to track how stars in the center of our Milky Way move across the sky, which can reveal how that region formed. They combined three sets of images taken over roughly ten years with the DECam camera, corrected for the camera's distortions, and measured the slow drift of about 48,000 stars in one camera chip's worth of sky. The stars' motions and their brightness-colour pattern were then used to separate bulge stars from nearby foreground stars.
summary.why: The measurements are said to match Gaia DR3 and HST studies while reaching about 1.5 magnitudes deeper than Gaia, which matters for studying faint bulge stars in crowded fields. The authors also note that the LSST camera uses the same CCD technology, so the calibration approach may help future Rubin Observatory work; the text does not show how far this method generalises beyond this single field.

papers.abstract: A complete characterization of the Galactic bulge stellar populations could offer important clues on the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. However, most bulge fields are hampered by high stellar crowding, strong interstellar extinction, and by heavy contamination from foreground disk stars. We aim to derive proper motions (PMs) towards the Baade's window by using DECam observations, extending kinematic studies of the Galactic bulge below the turn-off to a much larger field of view. We combined three datasets observed with DECam in the $r$-band spanning a ${\sim}$ 10-year baseline. As a pilot study, we only analyzed the field covered by a single detector. We developed an astrometric calibration pipeline that corrects for the DECam tree-ring pattern and residual distortions, tying all positions to the Gaia DR3 reference frame, and used them to derive PMs. We isolated the bulge population through a strict cut in $μ_{\ell^\ast}$, refined with a Gaia DR3 parallax selection. We measured PMs for $48\,239$ stars in the pilot field, with a median uncertainty of $0.65$ mas yr$^{-1}$ at $r_0<18$ mag. Our PMs agree closely with Gaia DR3, and reaches ${\sim}1.5$ magnitudes deeper than Gaia and a comparable depth to VIRAC2 in terms of relative completeness. We found velocity dispersions along Galactic longitude and latitude of $σ_{μ_{\ell^\ast}}=2.76\pm0.03$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and $σ_{μ_b}=2.49\pm0.02$ mas yr$^{-1}$ for the Galactic bulge, consistent with HST studies. We estimated a foreground contamination of ${\sim}14\%$ before any kinematic selection. The cleaned color-magnitude diagram reaches below the main-sequence turnoff, and shows no evidence for a large population younger than ${\sim}4$-$5$ Gyr in this field. Moreover, since the LSST camera shares the same CCD technology as DECam, this work offers a valuable precursor for crowded-field astrometry in the Rubin era.

papers.title: Chemical Cartography Across Time: The Age-Dependent Chemical Structure of the Milky Way with a Homogeneous Sample of 580,000 Giants from Five Surveys
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26550v1

summary.background:
- Galaxy disk: the flat, spinning part of the Milky Way where most stars, including the Sun, sit.
- Giant stars: evolved, bright stars whose light can be measured across large distances, which makes them useful for mapping.
- Metallicity ([Fe/H]): the share of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium in a star, here measured through iron relative to hydrogen. Stars formed later usually have more of it.
- Radial gradient: how a quantity changes with distance from the galactic centre, quoted here in dex per kiloparsec (dex is a logarithmic unit; a kiloparsec is about 3,260 light-years).
- Alpha elements ([Mg/Fe]): a chemical ratio used to separate the older, puffier thick disk (high-alpha) from the younger thin disk (low-alpha).
- Inside-out formation: the idea that the inner disk formed first and the outer disk later.
- Radial migration: stars drifting from their birthplace to other radii over time.
- Spectroscopic survey: a project that measures the light spectrum of many stars to infer their temperature, composition and other properties.
summary.one_liner: Using about 580,000 giant stars from five spectroscopic surveys, placed on one consistent parameter scale, the paper maps how the Milky Way's radial metallicity gradient and [Mg/Fe] gradient vary with stellar age.
summary.plain: The paper asks how the chemical makeup of our Galaxy varies from its centre outward, and whether that pattern has changed over time. The authors combined star measurements from five large sky surveys, all put on one common scale with one model, so their ages and element measurements can be compared directly. They report that the outward change in iron-to-hydrogen content is gentle for the youngest stars, steepest for stars of roughly 5 to 6 billion years, and nearly flat for the oldest stars.
summary.why: The result constrains how the Milky Way's disk built up, which matters for models of galaxy formation in general. The authors interpret it as consistent with inside-out growth, with the oldest stars possibly formed in a well-mixed disk or moved by radial migration; the text does not settle which explanation is right.

papers.abstract: Mapping the distribution of elements in the Milky Way and understanding how that distribution has changed over time can give us insight into the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. Here we use homogeneously estimated atmospheric parameters, elemental abundances, distances, and ages for ~580,000 giants from five major spectroscopic surveys---all simultaneously placed on a single, self-consistent scale by one model---allowing us, for the first time, to use a large sample of stars with uniform labels and ages that cumulatively span much of the disk to trace how the metallicity structure of the Milky Way depends on stellar age. Our chrono-chemical analysis shows that the radial metallicity gradient of the disk depends non-monotonically on age: it is shallow for the youngest stars, steepening to a maximum of ~-0.07 dex/kpc at intermediate ages (~5-6 Gyr), and flattening to near zero for the oldest stars. This "U-shaped" age dependence is driven largely by the low-alpha (thin-disk) population, with the high-alpha (thick-disk) sequence having weak gradients at all ages. In contrast to [Fe/H], the radial [Mg/Fe] gradient is weak (<~0.01 dex/kpc) at all ages. Together, these trends are consistent with an inside-out formation scenario in which the gradient of the star-forming gas has flattened over at least the last ~6 Gyr, while the near-zero gradient of the oldest stars reflects their formation in a well-mixed disk, efficient radial migration, or both.

papers.title: The Cosmic Infrared Background from Population III.1 Supermassive Stars and Black Holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25355v1

summary.background:
- Cosmic infrared background (CIB): the diffuse glow of infrared light from all sources over cosmic history, which is hard to separate into individual sources.
- Population III stars: the first generation of stars, made of pristine hydrogen and helium with no heavier elements.
- Supermassive black hole (SMBH): a black hole with millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, found at the centres of large galaxies.
- Seeding: the idea that early black holes grew from smaller "seed" black holes formed from collapsing early stars.
- Dark matter annihilation heating: dark matter particles colliding and releasing energy, which can keep early gas clouds hot and stop them fragmenting into small stars, allowing very massive stars to form.
- Eddington ratio: how fast a black hole is accreting matter compared with the maximum rate its radiation pressure allows; 0.01 means accreting at about 1% of that limit.
- Redshift z: a measure of distance and lookback time; z of about 6 to 20 corresponds to the first few hundred million to about a billion years after the Big Bang.
- Lyman-alpha: a specific ultraviolet/optical emission line of hydrogen that can be scattered by neutral hydrogen in intergalactic space.
summary.one_liner: This paper models the cosmic infrared background expected from a hypothesized Pop III.1 pathway in which supermassive primordial stars, heated by dark matter annihilation, seed early supermassive black holes, and tests the predicted background against existing observational limits.
summary.plain: The paper asks how much faint infrared light the universe should contain if the first giant black holes formed from enormous early stars powered partly by dark matter. The authors model light from those stars, from the black holes' accretion disks, from surrounding glowing gas, and from hydrogen Lyman-alpha radiation scattered through the neutral gas between galaxies. They then compare the totals with existing measurements of this background.
summary.why: Measurements of the infrared background are a rare indirect check on very early star and black hole formation that is hard to see directly. The text says the stellar part of the signal in its fiducial model is under 1% of existing measurements, while black hole accretion could be larger at average Eddington ratios near 0.01, and current data limit that ratio to about 0.3 or less. Whether this scenario holds up depends on the underlying model of Petkova et al. (2026), which this text does not evaluate.

papers.abstract: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating. We model the emission from Pop III.1 supermassive stars, including their growth phase, flash ionization phase, and early black hole accretion phase, as well as accompanying emission from lower-mass Pop III.2 stars. The CIB is composed of stellar and SMBH accretion disk continuum radiation, nebular continuum emission, and Ly$α$ radiation redistributed through scattering in the neutral intergalactic medium. Based on the feedback regulated Pop III.1 model of Petkova et al. (2026), our fiducial model assumes $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ Pop III.1 stars forming by $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with a comoving number density of $\sim0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$. For this model, the combined stellar contribution is less than $1\%$ of existing direct and diffuse CIB measurements. However, the contribution to the CIB from $z\sim6-20$ SMBH accretion is expected to be larger than the Pop III.1 stellar component for average Eddington ratios $λ_{\text{Edd}} \sim 0.01$. Latest CIB observations place constraints of $λ_{\text{Edd}} \lesssim 0.3$ for the fiducial Pop III.1 model during these epochs.

papers.title: The HI Mass Fractions of Milky Way Analog Samples
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25221v1

summary.background:
- HI: neutral atomic hydrogen, the cold gas from which stars can form, usually traced by its 21-cm radio emission.
- Stellar mass (M_star): the total mass of the stars in a galaxy.
- HI mass fraction (f_HI): the ratio of gas mass to stellar mass, a measure of how gas-rich a galaxy is relative to its stars.
- Milky Way analogs: other galaxies selected to be similar to our own in properties such as mass, size, or type.
- Global measurement: a whole-galaxy total, which is difficult for us to make from inside the Milky Way because we cannot view it from outside.
summary.one_liner: The paper estimates average neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) mass fractions for nine Milky Way analog galaxy samples and compares them with a recent Milky Way estimate.
summary.plain: Astronomers wanted to know how much cold atomic hydrogen gas the Milky Way holds compared with its stellar mass, and it is hard to measure this from inside our own galaxy. So they looked at groups of other galaxies chosen to resemble the Milky Way in various properties and averaged how much gas they hold relative to their stars. Most of these groups have less gas than a recent estimate for the Milky Way, though only the two largest differences are statistically significant.
summary.why: The gas-to-star ratio affects how galaxies form stars over time, so an unusual value for the Milky Way would be informative. The text does not settle which explanation is right: either the Milky Way is unusual, or the recent Milky Way gas estimate is too high.

papers.abstract: We estimate average HI mass fractions, f_HI = M_HI/M_star, for nine Milky Way analog samples (MWAs): galaxies selected on similarity to the MW in terms of various properties. We find most (seven) MWAs have lower <f_HI> than a recent estimate for the MW, although only the two largest have significantly lower estimates. We suggest that either the MW has an unusual f_HI for its properties, or we are overestimating its HI content, one of many challenging global measurements to make from our perspective inside our own Galaxy.

papers.title: Multi-epoch imaging observations of the Galactic Center with NIRCam and MIRI
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24110v1

summary.background:
- The Milky Way's center holds a supermassive black hole, a dense cluster of stars, and a nuclear stellar disk.
- The Central Molecular Zone is a dense band of gas and dust where stars form, with conditions similar to those in early-universe star-forming regions.
- JWST (James Webb Space Telescope) has two cameras named here: NIRCam (near-infrared) and MIRI (mid-infrared).
- Multi-epoch means repeat observations of the same field at different times, which reveal motion and change.
- Astrometric precision means how accurately star positions can be measured; photometric precision means how accurately brightness can be measured.
- Intermediate mass black holes sit between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes in size.
- Roman WFI is NASA's planned wide-field survey telescope, used here as a comparison.
- A Treasury Program is a large, public JWST program meant to serve the wider community.
summary.one_liner: This paper proposes a multi-epoch JWST Treasury program imaging the Galactic Center with NIRCam and MIRI over three epochs spaced three to five years apart, totaling about 420 hours.
summary.plain: The paper is a proposal for a long telescope program aimed at the center of our Milky Way, a crowded region around a supermassive black hole. The plan is to photograph the same area of sky three times, years apart, so that stars' tiny movements and brightness changes can be tracked. The text describes goals rather than results, since the observations have not yet been carried out.
summary.why: The Galactic Center is the closest galactic nucleus where individual stars can be resolved, so it offers a unique test case for star formation, black holes and planet-forming disks. The text says the program would go beyond the planned Roman survey in depth and precision, but it does not give measured outcomes to back this up.

papers.abstract: The center of the Milky Way is the densest and most extreme environment in our Galaxy, its most active star forming region, and the only galaxy nucleus where we can resolve stars down to about a solar mass on the main sequence. The Galactic Center (GC) contains a nuclear stellar disk, a nuclear star cluster, and a supermassive black hole, all embedded within the so-called Central Molecular Zone, which showcases conditions of the interstellar medium that are typically found in high-redshift star-forming regions. The GC hosts the highest concentration of massive stars in the Milky Way and hosts a large concentration of rare objects, such as Wolf Rayet stars and X-ray binaries. The GC is therefore an astrophysical target of outstanding importance. A multi-epoch JWST program enables novel science including the lifetime of planet-forming disks, the search for intermediate mass black holes, direct measurements of the multi-scale gravitational potential, and a deep measurement of the star formation history. Multi-epoch imaging observations with JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments will go far beyond Roman WFI surveys in terms of depth and astrometric and photometric precision because of its $3\times$ better resolution, and it expands spectral coverage in narrow bands and mid-infrared wavelength coverage. The proposed observations would correspond to a Treasury Program of about 420\,h, distributed over three epochs spaced three to five years apart.

papers.title: The Role of Galactic Shear in Regulating Local Star Formation Efficiency: A Combined MaNGA DynPop and ALMaQUEST Study
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22300v1

summary.background:
- Star formation efficiency (SFE): the fraction of molecular gas converted into stars per unit time, here measured per area.
- H-alpha emission: red light from hydrogen gas ionized by young hot stars, used as a star formation tracer (after correcting for dust).
- Molecular hydrogen traced via CO: carbon monoxide emission is the standard proxy for the H2 gas that forms stars.
- MaNGA: an optical survey that maps the light and motions of nearby galaxies spatially; DynPop is its dynamical modeling project.
- ALMaQUEST: a survey pairing MaNGA galaxies with ALMA radio observations of their molecular gas.
- Oort parameter A_Oort: a measure of differential rotation/shear in a galactic disk.
- Toomre stability: a parameter describing whether a rotating gas disk resists collapse into clumps.
- Mid-plane pressure: the pressure of gas at the disk's central plane, which affects cloud formation.
- Random forest regression: a machine-learning method that ranks which input variables best predict an outcome.
- Resolution limit: the smallest scale the data can resolve; cloud-scale processes lie below it.
summary.one_liner: Using MaNGA and ALMaQUEST data, the authors combine dynamical measurements with random forest regression to show that galactic shear (the Oort parameter A_Oort) is the dynamical property most associated with lower local star formation efficiency, mainly through its effect on radial trends, with gas density appearing to modulate that link.
summary.plain: Stars form from cold molecular gas, and this paper asks which conditions in a galaxy decide how efficiently that gas turns into stars, across small patches of nearby galaxies. The authors measured star formation from H-alpha light and molecular gas from carbon monoxide, then used a machine-learning method to rank which galaxy properties best predict the efficiency. Among the properties tested, the stretching force of galactic rotation (shear) was most associated with lower efficiency, though the predictions were only modest overall.
summary.why: It offers a measured link between large-scale galactic rotation and how well gas forms stars, which matters for models of star formation over galaxy lifetimes. The text does not show how far the result generalizes beyond the sampled galaxies, so its wider significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We study the local regulation of star formation efficiency (SFE) in star-forming regions of nearby galaxies using spatially resolved data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) and the ALMA-MaNGA QUEnching and STar formation (ALMaQUEST) surveys. We define the local SFE as $Σ_{\rm SFE} \equiv Σ_{\rm SFR}/Σ_{\rm H_2}$, where $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ is the star formation rate surface density derived from dust-corrected $\rm Hα$ emission, and $Σ_{\rm H_2}$ is the molecular hydrogen surface density derived from CO measurements. Combining these data with dynamical properties from the MaNGA DynPop project, we use random forest regression to identify the dominant factors of $Σ_{\rm SFE}$. Galactic shear, quantified by the Oort parameter $A_{\rm Oort}$, emerges as the dynamical property most strongly associated with lower SFE on average, exceeding the predictive power of mass surface density (either total or stellar), Toomre stability, and mid-plane pressure. However, these quantities provide only modest predictive power and primarily trace the radial variation of SFE. After removing the shear-related radial trends, only weak correlations remain between SFE and other local galactic properties, implying that the remaining azimuthal variations are likely governed by cloud-scale processes below our resolution limit. Furthermore, the relationship between SFE and shear varies among galaxies and weakens in gas-rich regions, suggesting that gas density may modulate the impact of shear. This behavior is consistent with competition between shear-induced cloud stabilization and shear-driven cloud-cloud collisions. Overall, galactic shear appears to regulate the large-scale radial distribution of SFE, while cloud-scale interstellar medium physics may drive the remaining variation.

papers.title: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23487v1

summary.background:
- Quasar: a supermassive black hole at a galaxy's center that is actively swallowing gas and shining very brightly.
- Feedback: energy from a black hole's winds or radiation that heats or blows away gas, which can stop a galaxy from forming new stars.
- Circumgalactic medium: diffuse gas surrounding a galaxy, out to its halo.
- Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect: hot electrons in gas slightly shift the cosmic microwave background light passing through them; the size of this shift measures the gas's total thermal energy.
- Redshift z=2.37: light is stretched by cosmic expansion; this corresponds to the universe at roughly 2.8 billion years old.
- Sigma (σ): a measure of statistical confidence; 6 sigma is a strong detection.
- Luminosity function: the count of galaxies at each brightness; its bright-end decline is a key test for galaxy formation models.
- Gyr, erg, kpc, solar mass: billion years, unit of energy, thousand parsecs, and mass of the Sun.
summary.one_liner: Reports a dual quasar at z=2.37 embedded in a hot gas bubble detected at 6 sigma via a thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich flux decrement, with a total thermal energy of 9.7e60 erg, plus hints of hot gas on 100-600 kpc scales.
summary.plain: Astronomers studied a pair of very bright, rapidly feeding black holes (quasars) seen as they were about 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang. They detected a large, hot, thin cloud of gas around them by how it slightly dims millimeter-wavelength light passing through it. They estimate the gas holds more heat energy than ordinary models of a halo of this mass would predict.
summary.why: If the result holds, it suggests quasar winds can heat and push gas far beyond their host galaxies, which is one proposed reason large galaxies are rarer than simple models predict. The text itself frames this as supporting evidence for feedback theory rather than a settled proof, and the link to the galaxy luminosity function is an interpretation the authors offer.

papers.abstract: Galaxy formation models necessitate that actively growing supermassive black holes, or quasars, strongly impact their environments. Theory suggests that quasar winds produce very hot gas bubbles that extend through the host galaxy and into the circumgalactic medium. Because this gas component is so hot and diffuse, the only way to measure its total energy is through the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect. Here we report the discovery of a dual quasar system at z=2.37 which is embedded in a bubble of hot gas as detected (at 6 $σ$) by a tSZ flux decrement at millimeter wavelengths. The total thermal energy of the hot gas is 9.7 x 10$^{60}$ erg. This energy exceeds the amount expected from all of the hot gas in a 10$^{13}$ M$_\odot$ dark matter halo by a factor of 3.6, and constitutes at least 0.6% of the quasar's lifetime energy output. We also find evidence for hot gas on larger (100-600 kpc) scales that may also originate in quasar outflows. This considerable excess energy is more than sufficient to shut off star formation and heat the intergalactic medium, implying a significant impact from quasar-driven winds on their surroundings. Such feedback plausibly explains the steep decline of the bright end of the luminosity function of galaxies across the observable Universe, and thus provides evidence to further support leading galaxy evolution theory.

papers.title: Active Galactic Nuclei as Beyond the Standard Model Laboratories: a White Paper
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21736v1

summary.background:
- AGN: a galaxy's central supermassive black hole actively pulling in matter, often outshining its host galaxy.
- Beyond the Standard Model (BSM): physics not captured by the current best theory of particles and forces, for example dark matter or new particles.
- Multi-messenger astronomy: combining different kinds of cosmic signals, such as light, neutrinos and gravitational waves.
- IceCube: a neutrino detector buried in Antarctic ice, which reported associating some neutrinos with individual AGN.
- Dark matter: unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effects, thought to surround galaxies and their black holes.
- White paper: a position or overview document summarising the state of a field, rather than presenting new results.
summary.one_liner: A white paper reviewing how multi-messenger and multi-wavelength observations of active galactic nuclei (AGN) could probe physics beyond the Standard Model, through the AGN themselves, the dark matter around them, and their interface, and listing open questions.
summary.plain: This paper looks at supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies that are feeding on gas, known as active galactic nuclei. The authors argue that watching these objects with several kinds of signals, such as light across wavelengths and particles like neutrinos, could reveal new physics that current theory does not cover. The text is a short review of the current state of research in this area, and it lists the main unanswered questions that need work before such discoveries become realistic.
summary.why: Interest has grown since IceCube linked neutrinos to individual AGN, which suggests these objects may act as natural particle-physics laboratories. The text does not report new measurements, so its value lies in organising a young, interdisciplinary field and its open questions.

papers.abstract: Multi-messenger and multi-wavelength observations of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can provide otherwise inaccessible knowledge about physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM), and may even lead to its discovery. Realizing this potential hinges on two parallel efforts: advancing our understanding of AGN and of the dark matter around them, and identifying the BSM signatures that are at once promising and robust against the gaps in that understanding. These fields have attracted growing interest in recent years, also motivated by the IceCube association of neutrinos to individual AGN, yet we have only begun to explore their cross-fertilization. This white paper offers a new perspective on this interdisciplinary endeavor. It concisely reviews the state of the art in each field and at their interface, and identifies the key open questions that must be addressed to strengthen our prospects for learning about BSM physics with AGN.

papers.title: Repeated Gravitational-Wave Lensing from Binary Black Holes on Eccentric and Precessing Orbits around Spinning Supermassive Black Holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20416v1

summary.background:
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects, detected as tiny signals in instruments.
- Black hole binary: two black holes orbiting each other; here a stellar-mass pair orbits a supermassive black hole, forming a hierarchical triple.
- Gravitational lensing: a massive object bends and focuses waves passing near it, which can amplify the signal; here the big black hole acts as the lens.
- LISA: a planned space-based gravitational-wave detector.
- Eccentricity and inclination: how elongated an orbit is and how tilted its plane is.
- Post-Newtonian dynamics: approximate corrections to Newtonian gravity used to model orbits near strong gravity.
- Fisher matrix: a standard statistical estimate of how precisely model parameters can be measured from a signal, not an actual measurement.
summary.one_liner: A simulation study of how repeated gravitational lensing of gravitational waves from a stellar-mass binary black hole orbiting a spinning supermassive black hole, on an eccentric and precessing outer orbit, could be identified and used to constrain parameters for LISA.
summary.plain: The paper looks at gravitational waves from a pair of black holes that orbit a much larger black hole at the centre of a galaxy. As the pair travels behind the big black hole, its signal can be bent and brightened, and this can happen more than once as the outer orbit changes shape and direction. The authors model this for a one-year observation by the planned LISA space detector and report how the timing and strength of these repeated lensing events depend on the outer orbit.
summary.why: Repeated lensing could give extra information about the big black hole's spin and the tilt of the outer orbit, which would be hard to get otherwise. The text reports these effects within a modelling framework, not observed data, so their real-world size depends on assumptions the summary does not fully spell out.

papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) from a stellar-mass binary black hole (BBH) orbiting a supermassive black hole (SMBH) can experience repeated gravitational lensing as the BBH passes behind the SMBH. Our previous studies of orbit-induced GW modulation motivate this investigation of repeated lensing in evolving hierarchical triple systems. We investigate how eccentricity, inclination, and relativistic precession of the outer orbit affect successive lensing events and parameter inference. The outer orbit follows post-Newtonian dynamics, and the inspiral waveform includes moving-source effects and de Sitter precession. An event-local point-mass lensing model tracks the changing source--lens alignment and GW frequency. For a one-year LISA observation, we examine lensing-event identification, Fisher-matrix estimates of parameter uncertainties, and waveform residuals when lensing is omitted. Our results show that outer-orbit evolution changes the timing and amplification of successive lensing events and can bring initially unfavorable configurations into the lensing region. A fixed circular, nonprecessing approximation misses all lensing events for a substantial fraction of the selected lensed systems. The median fractional reductions in uncertainty are largest for the outer-orbit inclination and SMBH spin. For some systems above the adopted detection threshold, lensing-induced waveform differences persist after local adjustments to the parameters of the unlensed model. Repeated lensing can thus provide complementary constraints on SMBH properties and outer-orbit geometry in LISA observations of hierarchical BBHs.
